answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher & statesman
answer.sourceLine: This is the documented opening thesis of Seneca’s essay On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae 1.3), which in Latin reads “Non exiguum temporis habemus, sed multum perdidimus.” The attribution to Seneca is not in doubt; the exact English is a translation — “waste much of it” matches John W. Basore’s 1932 Loeb rendering, while “short time to live” is C. D. N. Costa’s Penguin phrasing (in place of Basore’s “short space of time”).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae), §1.3
Seneca the Younger, addressed to Pompeius Paulinus
“waste much of it” follows John W. Basore, Loeb Classical Library, 1932

source.excerpt: Latin (1.3): “Non exiguum temporis habemus, sed multum perdidimus. Satis longa uita et in maximarum rerum consummationem large data est, si tota bene collocaretur.” — rendered by Basore (1932) as “It is not that we have a short space of time, but that we waste much of it. Life is long enough … if it were all well invested.”
trail: The wording is the famous opening argument of Seneca’s essay On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae 1.3), whose Latin reads “Non exiguum temporis habemus, sed multum perdidimus.”
The distinctive phrase “waste much of it” matches John W. Basore’s 1932 Loeb translation, quoted as “a short space of time, but that we waste much of it.”
The older public-domain translation by Aubrey Stewart (1889) phrases the same sentence differently — “we lose a great deal of it” — confirming the popular wording tracks a modern rendering.
source.excerptNote: The Latin has no word for “to live”; translators supply it. Popular English versions vary the verb — “waste much of it” (Basore), “waste a lot of it” (Costa), “lose a great deal of it” (Stewart).

author.name: Seneca (Lucius Annaeus Seneca)
author.heading: About Seneca
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman & dramatist
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (“Seneca the Younger”) was a Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman and tutor to the emperor Nero. His moral essays and Letters to Lucilius are among the most quoted works of Stoicism. On the Shortness of Life, addressed to Pompeius Paulinus around AD 49, argues that life is not too short — we simply squander it. Ordered to take his own life by Nero in AD 65, he did so with Stoic composure.

misattribution.heading: A note on the wording
misattribution.intro: This one is correctly credited to Seneca — unusual for a famous-name quote. The catch is the English: Seneca wrote in Latin, and the popular sentence is a translator’s rendering that no single standard edition reproduces word-for-word.

items.who: The exact English is a blend of translations
items.why: “Waste much of it” is John W. Basore’s 1932 Loeb wording, but Basore writes “short space of time,” not “short time to live.” The popular form pairs Basore’s verb with the “short time to live” phrasing of C. D. N. Costa’s Penguin translation.
You will also see “waste a lot of it” (C. D. N. Costa, Penguin) and “lose a great deal of it” (Aubrey Stewart, 1889) — all translating the same Latin sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is genuinely Seneca’s, from On the Shortness of Life 1.3: “Non exiguum temporis habemus, sed multum perdidimus.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: On the Shortness of Life opens by refusing a common complaint — that nature gives us too few years. Seneca’s inversion is the whole point of the essay: the trouble is not the length of life but our habit of frittering it away on ambition, busyness and other people’s demands.
Written to his kinsman Pompeius Paulinus, then in charge of Rome’s grain supply, the essay reads as a gentle argument that a life “well invested” is long enough for anything worth doing.
context.pull: “Non exiguum temporis habemus, sed multum perdidimus.”
